Senses.Explanation: ‘Old Master Wang’ is Nanquan Puyuan’s recurrent self-designation and the label under which later records quote him. Literally, Wang, old master or teacher. In the Chan record this is Nanquan Puyuan's recurrent self-designation and the label later writers use when quoting or commenting on him. The compound occurs 760 times in 193 allowlisted texts. Nanquan's biography identifies him as Puyuan, a son of the Wang family of Zhengzhou, and immediately records him saying, 'Old Master Wang is selling himself; is there anyone who will buy?' Other self-references include the water-buffalo saying, 'Old Master Wang has raised a water buffalo since he was young,' asking Zhaozhou, 'Where is Old Master Wang at fault?' and saying that Old Master Wang, unlike Mazu, does not say 'mind is buddha' but 'not mind, not buddha, not a thing.' Later comments preserve the title while explicitly naming Nanquan.
Senses.Note: This is a person-title, not a generic entry for every teacher surnamed Wang. The explicit biography and repeated Nanquan section headings fix its principal referent. The full name 'Nanquan Old Master Wang' occurs 17 times in 12 texts; the selling-himself phrase occurs 41 times in 37.

Senses.Explanation: To see one's own nature. Chan records place this claim in transmission formulas, instructions, questions, and explicit challenges. Hongren links it with directly becoming a buddha; a text attributed to Bodhidharma says that seeking a buddha requires it. Huangbo Xiyun answers a direct question by refusing to make nature a second object seen by a separate seeing subject. Dahui Zonggao repeats that it is required for an unerring road and immediately asks which mind recognizes and which nature is seen. Zhongfeng Mingben says direct pointing is no longer direct once it enters speech or contrivance, while Yongming Yanshou says that once nature is seen, mind and the teaching remedies both cease. The phrase names a claimed recognition, but the records repeatedly test what the grammar of a seer looking at a separate nature would wrongly add.

Senses.Explanation: The faculty or nature of seeing, a noun phrase rather than the action of seeing one's own nature. Hanyue Fazang and Bore Gulin each quote an outside claimant who treats this seeing faculty as an unchanging witness that survives the destruction of a visible tile or stove; both speakers identify that claim as an error. Senses.Explanation: To open one’s mouth is the visible onset of speaking, repeatedly made the exact pressure point of a Chan exchange. In the Guizong case an unnamed monk is struck precisely when he is about to open his mouth; in Xuedou Chongxian’s meeting with Zhimen, the second blow falls at the same instant. Yuanwu stops Kaifu Daoning as soon as he begins, while Dahui threatens a hot iron wheel at the mere move. Other addresses demand that the assembly open its mouths or direct recognition to what precedes opening mouth and raising intention. Foyin’s portrait verse turns an open-mouthed smile into a public question. Zen bends an ordinary bodily transition into the timed boundary where an answer is demanded, interrupted, struck, or forestalled.

Senses.Explanation: “Open your mouth and you are already wrong” is spoken as both self-verdict and interview challenge, commonly paired with losing by silence or missing as soon as the mind frames an answer. Literally, open the mouth and immediately or already be wrong : "open your mouth and you are already wrong." The phrase occurs 43 times in 34 allowlisted texts; the variant "open your mouth and it is then wrong" occurs 13 times in 10. Its early defining exchange has an unnamed questioner ask Dabe to speak apart from removing the upper and taking away the lower. Dabe answers, "when I open my mouth I am already wrong" . The unnamed questioner calls Dabe his guide; Dabe replies, "today I died in the disciple's hands" , so the record shows the verdict catching Dabe’s own utterance. Later masters make it a portable paired formula: Po'an says, "open your mouth and you are already wrong; aim the mind and you immediately miss" . Other records pair it with "move a thought and immediately go against" . Wuzhun states the closed-mouth counterpart, "open your mouth and you are already wrong; close your mouth and you are already lost," then asks how communication is possible apart from opening and not opening . The phrase also becomes an encounter instruction: Baishan tells an unnamed questioner, "open your mouth and you are already wrong; move a thought and immediately go against; leave these two roads and speak quickly!" The unnamed questioner answers, "wrong," and Baishan answers with another stock retort. Chan thus bends an ordinary judgment of erroneous speech into a self-applying verdict, a fixed parallel line, and a demand used while requiring an answer; the records preserve the resulting replies rather than defining silence as the solution.

Senses.Explanation: Chan records use this verb for an awakening event that breaks open in a person and, in direct address, for bringing listeners to that event. Lamp compilers narrate Guling Shenzan, Angulimala, an unnamed monk, and Ashvaghosha as persons who open into awakening after an encounter, words, or a sound. The actors undergo the event; they do not utter its lexical label. Yongming Yanshou stresses that the event admits no intervening instant, Mazu Daoyi uses the verb causatively for opening his listeners into awakening, and Zhongfeng Mingben speaks of a time when it occurs naturally in sustained inquiry. Intransitive and causative syntax retain one core event while changing who undergoes or brings it about.

Senses.Explanation: To disclose or show something, including instruction shown in a public interview. An unnamed monk asks Baizhang Yuansu to disclose the intention of the patriarch’s coming from the west and receives “the mud ox swallows the huge wave”; the named layman He Changbai asks Juelang Daosheng for instruction for the Fushan assembly and receives a verse about clouds and snow. In the Longtan–Tianhuang case, Longtan Chongxin complains that he has long attended without being shown the essentials of mind. Tianhuang Daowu lists raising a hand when tea was brought and lowering his head when greeted, then asks, “Where was I not showing you the essentials of mind?” (那裏不是與你開示心要處). The Blue Cliff Record's compiler narrates that Jingqing Daofu used a responsive dynamic to “show later students” (開示後學); Jingqing is the person described, not the utterer of that clause. The monastery manager Chengyi tells Jifei Ruyi that he has received Jifei’s disclosure (承師開示), treating Jifei’s reply as instruction already given. Request, act, repeated conduct, and received instruction are stages of the same showing, not different lexical referents.
